001.title: Kickoff: throwing ideas at the wall

paragraphs.text: First team meeting. We compared the assignment requirements, discussed possible themes, and drafted our first task split. We considered video game characters, the most wanted hackers, and a professional team portfolio. Nothing quite convinced us.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: we had ideas, but none had a strong identity.

paragraphs.label: Decision
paragraphs.text: leave the theme open for one more day and have each person bring a developed proposal.

paragraphs.label: Lesson of the day
paragraphs.text: aimless debate wastes time. It's better to bring well-developed ideas.

002.title: The Festival (and World Tour) is born

paragraphs.text: Each team member presented an idea. The winner: a music festival website. It let us explore a bold visual style, animations, artist cards, and even a merch store. Then came the idea that defined the project: a journal styled as World Tour dates. Each date would be a development milestone; each city, a new stage.
At the same meeting, we chose the color palette, typefaces, responsibilities, and GitHub repository.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: we couldn't agree on a palette (some wanted black, others wanted minimalism).

paragraphs.label: Solution
paragraphs.text: a quick vote settled it: vibrant colors and a light background best captured the festival feel.

003.title: First commits and the classic 'no, this is better'

paragraphs.text: Initial repository setup: folder structure, README, branches, and the first commit.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: we debated whether the HTML files should go in a folder for better organization.

paragraphs.label: Solution
paragraphs.text: rereading the assignment made it clear they had to stay in the root. End of discussion.

004.title: From tour dates to concert tickets

paragraphs.text: A long, productive day. The visual style was settled, the index was 90% done, and we started structuring each team member's profile.
Here's the twist: we finished the whole journal in a World Tour dates format... and didn't like it. 😅

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: the World Tour idea looked nice on paper, but felt boring when rendered: too much like a schedule, just a list of dates. It needed more energy.

paragraphs.label: Solution
paragraphs.text: we redesigned it completely. Each journal entry became a concert ticket, changing the tone from an agenda to a memory of an epic night.

005.title: Hunting bugs that weren't there yesterday (or so we thought)

paragraphs.text: The project woke up with a fresh coat of paint and an army of bugs underneath. They weren't appearing out of nowhere; we just hadn't seen them before. Now we had, and they kept us busy.

paragraphs.label: The hamburger menu
paragraphs.text: desktop looked elegant; on mobile it didn't cover the whole div, and the tiny text was hard to tap.

paragraphs.label: The animations
paragraphs.text: the image movement looked great, but broke margins on devices.

paragraphs.label: Lessons learned
paragraphs.text: a bug isn't 'weird'; it's a bug we don't understand yet. If it hasn't been tested on a real mobile device, it isn't tested. Animations need boundaries: overflow, transform-origin, and breakpoints. The hamburger menu isn't a component; it's an ecosystem.
Bugs everywhere. But we kept going.
With the whole site built, we looked back at the journey: from having no theme to having a complete festival with a lineup, profiles, and the journal you're reading.
Splitting work by branch went well, but we also learned to check with the group before editing a shared file (css/base.css gave us a few merge-conflict headaches).

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: with so many last-minute changes, coordinating who pushed what and in which order was difficult.

paragraphs.label: Solution
paragraphs.text: we created a shared final checklist so everyone could tick off their task before pushing and avoid overwriting each other's work.

007.title: Second edition: the festival returns, now in React

paragraphs.text: The TP2 assignment arrived: move the project to React, with a shared sidebar, local JSON data, a public API, the component tree, and this journal.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: we had to decide what to reuse from TP1 and what to rebuild from scratch.

paragraphs.label: Decision
paragraphs.text: keep the festival identity (palette, typefaces, cards, and tickets) and rebuild the structure with components. The band lineup and venue weather fit the theme while covering JSON and API requirements.

008.title: From four HTML files to one component

paragraphs.text: We created the project with Vite and React Router, and turned TP1's top menu into a fixed sidebar that marks the active section.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: in TP1 each profile was a separate HTML file with the same structure copied four times. Every change had to be repeated.

paragraphs.label: Decision
paragraphs.text: one profile component receives each team member's data from members.json. The TP1 interactions (hype meter, recommender, player, and quotes) became their own components.

paragraphs.label: Lesson of the day
paragraphs.text: repeated things become components; changing things become props.
With the structure underway, we had to choose tools for each part from the options covered in class.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: we could use fetch or Axios for API requests, and Bootstrap, CSS Modules, styled-components, or our own stylesheets. Each choice changed how the code would be written.

paragraphs.label: Decision
paragraphs.text: fetch with async/await and try/catch, since it's built into the browser and adds no dependencies. We chose section-specific stylesheets to keep TP1's look without relying on a library.
Our first complete run of the app locally: home page, profiles, lineup, weather, component tree, and journal.

paragraphs.label: Change request
paragraphs.text: the sidebar took up too much space on desktop. We added a button to collapse it to icons; on mobile it still works as a panel.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: an API that requires a key exposes it in a public repository, while others don't allow browser requests (CORS).

paragraphs.label: Solution
paragraphs.text: we chose Open-Meteo: no key needed, works in the browser, and lets us show loading and error messages with a retry button.
We checked the lineup at different screen sizes and found two details that threw off the poster.

paragraphs.label: Problem
paragraphs.text: the cards had different heights: a long name like "Los Fabulosos Cadillacs" wrapped to two lines and stretched only that card. The "More info" details also opened inside the card and disrupted the grid.

paragraphs.label: Decision
paragraphs.text: each row now matches the tallest card, with the button always at the bottom. Band details open in a modal (BandModal) above the lineup.

paragraphs.label: Lesson of the day
paragraphs.text: the browser's <dialog> element handles much of accessibility: it traps focus, dims the background, and closes with Escape. We only added closing via ✕ and clicking outside.

tree.main: Entry point: mounts React in the <div id="root"> and wraps the app in BrowserRouter.
tree.app: Defines routes with React Router. All routes share the same Layout.
tree.layout: Shared structure for every screen. Stores whether the sidebar is collapsed and renders the page for the current route in its <Outlet />.
tree.sidebar: Shared side menu: team identity, NavLinks, and active section. It collapses to icons on desktop and opens as a panel on mobile.
tree.splashes: Decorative background shapes using the lineup colors.
tree.outlet: React Router renders one of these pages here, depending on the URL.
tree.home: Home page: team introduction, flip cards, and a random profile.
tree.artist-card: A card for each team member. The same component is reused four times with different props.
tree.profile: Reads the URL slug and looks up the team member's data in members.json.
tree.profile-view: Builds a profile from the data received through props.
tree.pick-list: Numbered favorites list: one for movies and one for albums.
tree.interaction: Renders the interaction specified by each member's "interaction" field.
tree.skills: Sebas: interactive skill bars from levels 1 to 5, with a message at the maximum.
tree.random: Valen: random movie or album recommendation.
tree.player: Agus: a pretend player for his favorite albums.
tree.quotes: Celi: quote generator featuring Spanish-language authors.
tree.profile-not-found: Only shown when the slug doesn't match a team member.
tree.cartelera: Displays lineup.json with text search and genre filters.
tree.band-card: A card for each matching band, with a button to view more information.
tree.band-modal: Modal with band details. Only rendered when a band is selected.
tree.weather: Fetches the Open-Meteo API and handles loading, error, and success states.
tree.weather-result: Current weather and a 3-day forecast, shown only after a successful request.
tree.render-tree: This section. Draws the tree from componentTree.js data.
tree.tree-node: Each tree node. It calls itself to render its children.
tree.bitacora: Process journal with assignment filters and expandable tickets.
tree.ticket-entry: Each journal entry, styled like a concert ticket.
tree.merch-card: An item in the official store.
tree.back-to-top: Floating button to return to the top.
